# Aloud

> A free browser tool that does three jobs on one script: reads text aloud in a chosen
> voice, runs that text as a scrolling teleprompter, and transcribes speech to text by
> dictation. No account, no installation, no usage limit.

Aloud runs entirely on the Web Speech API built into the browser, so text-to-speech and
teleprompter use cost nothing and work offline.

## Languages

The interface ships in English (https://aloud.app/), Spanish (/es/), French (/fr/),
German (/de/), Arabic (/ar/) and Simplified Chinese (/zh/). Each is a separate static
page with its own metadata and hreflang alternates.

The tool reads and dictates in any language the device has a voice installed for, which
is independent of the interface language. Right-to-left scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian,
Urdu) are laid out right-to-left. Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Thai are counted and
paced by character rather than word, because they are not written with spaces, and the
teleprompter dial switches from words per minute to characters per minute for them.
Speech-duration estimates use per-language character rates rather than one global
words-per-minute figure.

## The three modes

- **LISTEN (text to speech / read aloud)**: the machine speaks and the user listens. Every
  voice installed on the device is selectable and auditionable. A lime marker slides
  word-by-word beneath the text as it is spoken, so the user can read along. Speech rate
  (0.5x–2x) and pitch are adjustable.
- **PROMPT (teleprompter)**: the user speaks. No synthetic voice is involved. The script
  scrolls continuously to hold the current line at a fixed reading height, paced in words
  per minute (default 130). Longer words are held longer so the pacing drifts like real
  speech. Includes a mirror toggle for beam-splitter prompter glass and a fullscreen mode.
- **DICTATE (speech to text)**: the user speaks and the words become the script, which can
  then be read back or run through the teleprompter.

## Key facts

- Free, no sign-up, no installation, no API key.
- Text-to-speech and teleprompter run fully on-device; pasted text is never uploaded.
- Dictation is the exception: Chrome and Edge stream microphone audio to their own speech
  servers to transcribe it. Confidential material should not be dictated.
- Audio cannot be exported as MP3. The browser speech engine plays audio directly and
  exposes no recordable stream; that requires a cloud text-to-speech service.
- No length limit and no trimming. Long scripts are split into sentence-sized pieces
  internally, which also avoids a Chrome bug that cuts speech off after about 15 seconds.
- The voice list comes from the operating system, so it differs between macOS, Windows,
  Android and iOS. More voices can be installed in system settings.
- Any language with an installed voice is supported; the cast voice also sets the language
  dictation listens for.
- The waveform in the transport is generated from the script itself: letter density drives
  the peaks and punctuation cuts visible dips, so sentence breaks are readable. It is
  clickable to jump to any word.

## Terminology

Text to speech, read aloud and teleprompter are commonly conflated but differ by who is
speaking. Text to speech: the machine speaks, the user listens. Read aloud: text to speech
plus a synced on-screen highlight. Teleprompter: the user speaks and the machine only
paces the script. Speech to text (dictation) is the reverse direction entirely.

## Browser support

Text to speech: Chrome, Edge, Safari and most modern browsers. Teleprompter: all browsers,
since it needs no speech engine. Dictation: Chrome and Edge, plus recent Safari.
